content:
Earlier this year, I swapped a gasoline-powered mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. The user can manually drive the robot along the edge of the lawn to build a virtual map. Once setup is complete, the robot will mow automatically according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tested another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different approach to navigation, and after several weeks of testing, I think this machine may be easier for many people to use.

Camera-assisted automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 that I reviewed earlier this year is how each understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to drive the mower along the border with my phone before it could build an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses what the manufacturer calls the TerraVision 2.0 system. Equipped with three cameras, the mower can automatically map out the lawn area, with no need to bury boundary wires underground or install an extra RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who are less comfortable with computer technology.

To verify this, I asked my mum, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any help from me along the way. She said everything worked fine. That said, I'm not entirely sure she would have had the patience to first drive the robot along the entire border with her phone, and then mark out all the areas that need to be avoided.

During the automatic mapping process in my front yard, a couple of small issues came up. There is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, so the TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's grass in my map.

I set that area as a no-go zone in the app, and the problem was resolved. That said, if there is no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, you need to be especially careful when building the initial map.

A look through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also enable one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used my iPhone's screen mirroring feature to cast that video onto the big screen of my Mac. I could sit indoors working while watching from the mower's point of view as it moved around the backyard.

This feature is not necessary for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun, and sometimes explains why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not have a corresponding camera live view feature.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps share many features. Both support preset schedules, mowing mode adjustments, zone划分, no-go zone marking, and remote control of the mower.

The TerraMow is especially thoughtfully designed when it comes to the last feature. In addition to the traditional left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule, with no human intervention. That said, the TerraMow's joystick mode is quite handy for tidying up small patches the robot may have missed.

Sometimes I almost feel like I'm controlling the robot with telekinesis (the fun kind). I walk behind the mower holding my iPhone, give a gentle push with my thumb, and the robot goes exactly where I direct it.

Every robotic mower app should copy this design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut the grass closer to the ground and was also noticeably louder while running.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow "noisy," but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly — even if it comes out at night with its headlights on, you can almost forget it's still operating.

Because the TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. For that reason, scheduling daytime mowing becomes more important.

The V1000 feels solidly built and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage in the box, which can cover the charging dock, whereas the Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently reliable. I left it to mow every day for several weeks in a row, and it never needed any human intervention.

When adaptive mapping is a little too "smart"

The same kind of visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continually adjusts the map based on what it sees. After each job, saving these changes takes a rather long time, during which you can't do anything in the app.

After several days of heavy rain in a row, I ran into an interesting edge case. Water had pooled in one spot of the yard, and the TerraMow cleverly avoided that area during its next run.

Inside the circular area that was skipped, the weeds grew taller and taller. After a while, the mower seemed to mistake the taller weeds there for something that needed to be avoided permanently, and even after the ground dried out, that area kept being skipped.

I used the app's remote control feature to manually drive the mower over there and cut down the taller grass, and the problem was resolved. Once that area returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed there as well.

Regular edging also helps the TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. Otherwise, tall grass growing along a模糊 boundary may be mistaken for an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

The Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more heavily on boundaries and obstacles that the user defines themselves. That method requires more preparation, but it avoids situations where the map "changes its mind" about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac conclusion

After using both systems, for most people, I lean toward recommending the TerraMow's camera-led approach.

For me, burying wires in the ground is completely impractical, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining extra hardware. The TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. The initial mapping takes longer,模糊 boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook an overgrown patch of weeds for a permanent obstacle.

All of these issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, an engaging camera live view, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I have used.

I really enjoy tending the garden, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this chore over to a robot frees up time to look after flower beds, do edging, and handle detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 performs excellently in this regard, and I would recommend it, especially for users who want a robotic mower but don't want to bury wires underground, don't want to install an RTK antenna, and don't want to walk the entire yard holding their phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at $999, available with a $200 coupon code on deal sites. The product can also be purchased from the TerraMow official website.
